title: MemVanta: Memory-Efficient CPU Inference for Quantized GGUF Language Models
summary: Deploying large language models on commodity CPUs is often constrained not only by computational throughput but also by the resident memory required to execute quantized models within fixed system budgets. We present MemVanta, an experimental C++20 inference runtime for quantized GGUF language models that treats memory residency as a first-class systems objective. MemVanta combines memory-mapped model access, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution paths, paged key-value state, and explicit memory-pressure validation. We evaluate MemVanta against a pinned this http URL baseline using the same OpenLLaMA 7B v2 Q4_0 GGUF under CPU-only execution. Across five measured runs following warm-up, MemVanta records a peak resident set size of 3,983,412 KiB compared with 7,586,960 KiB for this http URL , corresponding to a 47.50 percent reduction in peak RSS. This memory reduction involves a substantial throughput trade-off: MemVanta achieves 3.15 +/- 0.04 tokens/s for prompt processing and 1.52 +/- 0.02 tokens/s for token generation, compared with 45.82 +/- 0.96 and 7.76 +/- 0.09 tokens/s, respectively, for this http URL . In a separate Linux cgroup-v2 experiment with swap disabled, MemVanta completes execution at a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling, while this http URL is OOM-killed at that ceiling and first succeeds at the tested 3840 MiB level. These results position MemVanta as a memory-efficiency research prototype rather than a throughput competitor. We analyze the architectural mechanisms underlying this trade-off and discuss reproducibility, correctness, limitations, and opportunities for memory-constrained CPU and edge inference.

title: Adaptive Warm-State Retention for Serverless Cold-Start Mitigation: Treating Keep-Alive Time as an Online Control Parameter
summary: Serverless platforms are easy to operate but pay a recurring price in cold starts: when a function is called after sitting idle, its execution environment must be rebuilt before the request can run, and latency suffers. The usual fix keeps idle environments alive for a fixed window, but a single value rarely fits a changing workload: too high wastes idle capacity, too low causes avoidable cold starts. We argue the keep-alive window should not be a fixed deployment constant; instead we treat it as a per-function runtime parameter, adjusted online from what the system observes, kept separate from how many replicas to run. We build an external retention controller for OpenFaaS/faasd that needs no platform changes, driven by two simple agents: a reactive AIMD (Additive-Increase Multiplicative-Decrease) rule and a UCB1 multi-armed bandit. Against fixed-timeout baselines and a predictive histogram keep-alive, on steady, bursty, and trace-derived workloads (Huawei Serverless 2023), the bandit cuts the aggregate cold-start rate from 63% under immediate scale-to-zero to 3%, holds P95 tail latency at the level of the longest-retention fixed baseline, and uses about 13% less accumulated warm time than that baseline, while also beating the predictive baseline. No fixed timeout is best on every metric, whereas the adaptive agents reach a favorable operating point without manual tuning; on the bursty workload at a converged horizon the bandit's advantage is statistically significant. On a multi-node Kubernetes cluster under the platform's own Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, the controller coexists with an autoscaler it does not control: the replica count follows load identically across policies, and retention independently governs warm time.

title: CCAMoE: Cache-Conditioned Adaptive Inference for Offloaded MoE
summary: Expert offloading enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained GPUs, but expert transfers and CPU execution limit decoding performance. Speculative decoding can mitigate these costs, yet separate draft weights consume scarce GPU memory and longer drafts increase verification demand. In this paper, we present CCAMoE, a unified runtime that coordinates adaptive speculative decoding with concurrent expert-cache updates. Its design has three key features: 1) Cache-only drafting, which reuses resident target experts to generate proposals and routing hints without separate draft weights; 2) Draft-guided cache updates, which anticipate expert demand and overlap transfers with computation to support subsequent drafting and verification; and 3) Cost-aware draft-length control, which balances expected acceptance against execution cost. Together, these mechanisms coordinate proposal generation and cache preparation through a shared evolving cache, improving proposal quality while reducing verification cost. Across various MoE models, GPU platforms, and workloads, CCAMoE consistently achieves the lowest decoding latency, with up to 2.33$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Making Repeated Variational Circuit Optimization Efficient on GPUs
summary: Repeated numerical optimization is a defining workload for classical simulation of parameterized quantum circuits. Although successive training steps change gate parameters, they usually preserve circuit connectivity and reuse a small set of gate-layer patterns. We use this regularity to accelerate gradient evaluation on GPUs. Our framework combines execution primitives for common circuit layers with adjoint differentiation, coordinating state evolution and derivative computation to reduce launch overhead, intermediate storage, and state-vector traffic. Because effective schedules depend on circuit size, gate structure, and device resources, our framework retains several execution choices instead of committing to a single schedule. Structural and hardware constraints narrow these choices, after which measurements on representative layers guide plan selection. The selected plans are reused while circuit structure remains fixed, spreading the selection cost over repeated training iterations. This approach targets the computation required by optimization rather than forward simulation alone, while retaining the numerical semantics of state-vector differentiation. Experiments across multiple circuit families and GPU platforms compare our framework with the native GPU adjoint implementation in PennyLane Lightning. The results demonstrate substantially lower gradient evaluation times over the evaluated workloads, together with the numerical accuracy checks reported in the evaluation.

title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
summary: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.

title: When Does Decomposition Help? Empirical Study on Workload-Architecture Affinity in LLM Inference Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference can be organized as independent monolithic replicas, tensor- or pipeline-parallel serving groups, or disaggregated prefill and decode services. Although decomposition is often presented as a route to higher efficiency, its benefit depends on workload shape, model fit, and whether phase-specific resources can be independently scaled. Existing comparisons frequently change several of these factors at once. We isolate the architectural effect by evaluating five SGLang serving organizations under the same four-A100-40GB hardware envelope, pinned Qwen3-8B model, software stack, prompts, and arrival schedules. Our evaluation contains 150 audited conditions over short-chat, decode-heavy, and 32K prefill-heavy workloads. Four independent one-GPU replicas achieve the lowest end-to-end latency for short chat and long output and are the only architecture stable in every condition. Pipeline parallelism reduces 32K time to first token by 58-59% at non-stress rates, while hybrid pipeline-based disaggregation achieves the best 32K end-to-end latency at 0.4 requests/s. In contrast, B's single-VM static TP2+TP2 split, without independent phase scaling, does not improve tested latency over replication and collapses at higher 32K load. These results reveal a workload-architecture affinity: pipeline decomposition favors prefill-heavy computation, whereas replication favors decode-heavy and concurrent traffic. More broadly, decomposition is not a monotonic optimization; its value depends on matching parallelism granularity to the dominant phase and preserving queue stability.

title: Ossim: OS-Driven Live Simulation for Cluster-Scale Full-Stack Evaluation (Extended Version)
summary: Cluster-scale full-stack simulation is essential for evaluating distributed software stacks and emerging hardware components before deployment. Such simulation must achieve both full-stack fidelity for the unmodified production stack and the simulation performance required for iterative configuration exploration. However, no existing method achieves both. We present Ossim, an OS-level approach to cluster-scale full-stack simulation built on top of the Linux virtualization stack. Ossim comprises four subsystems: simulation-oriented scheduling, live memory hierarchy management, simulation-aware IPC, and multi-host coordination. Together, they coordinate live and modeled components under shared simulated time while controlling interference among co-located live VMs. These mechanisms point toward simulation-native OS support, where simulation control and orchestration become core OS responsibilities.
comment: Extended version of the APSys'26 paper ( arXiv:2606.18958 ). 14 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables

title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
summary: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

title: LiZoneDedup: An End-to-End In-Storage Deduplication Architecture for ZNS SSDs
summary: Data deduplication reduces write traffic and extends flash lifetime, especially on versioned workloads: container images, VM snapshots, and backups. Yet in-storage deduplication has never been implemented for emerging Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs. Conventional designs require a page-level FTL to remap duplicate writes and a device-wide fingerprint index far exceeding controller DRAM; neither exists under ZNS. Our insight is that ZNS's append-only contract is a natural substrate for deduplication: a duplicate mapping, once recorded, is never modified in place, so dedup metadata becomes an append-only log rather than a mutable page-level table, and fingerprints fit in compact per-zone indexes rather than a global index. We present \sysname, the first complete in-storage deduplication architecture for ZNS, built around three mechanisms: a device-selected write primitive that hides zone placement from the host, content-based routing that confines each lookup to a small fixed set of candidate zones, and lifecycle-separated metadata with per-zone identity indexes and append-only reference counts. On a 1\,TB ZNS SSD, \sysname replaces the $\sim$10.7 GB global fingerprint index with per-zone indexes of a few hundred KB that become NAND-resident once sealed, holds controller DRAM at 37-50 MB (including a bounded-size metadata LRU cache) regardless of device capacity, improves logical write throughput by 1.1-3.5$\times$, cuts physical writes by up to 85\%, and reaches 91-99\% of the throughput of an infeasible page-FTL oracle.

title: CXL Coherence Writes Back What Surviving Hosts See, Leaving Flushes Only for Ordering
summary: Hosts that share memory over Compute Express Link (CXL) cache its lines, and a host that crashes loses the lines it has modified and not written back. Designs for such memory stop every host when one crashes, assume stored energy, or flush after each operation. We show that when a crashing host's clients die with it, the flushes a host crash requires are those that keep one line from reaching the memory device before a line it depends on, and not those that make a finished operation durable. The reason is a property that CXL requires of the fabric: a modified line is written back before another host accesses it. Whatever a surviving host has seen is then on the device, and our crash condition lets a crash drop operations that only the crashed host observed. We prove the claim for operations that take effect in a single store, and test it on small instances of models of three published designs, whose operations store several times. A lock table needs no flush to keep the locks of surviving hosts. A persistent hash index keeps every operation a survivor has observed, and in two workloads it writes fewer than half as many lines to the device as its published code does. An allocator's flush of each new reference is neither sufficient nor necessary for the survivors' safety: the allocator lacks ordering flushes, one of them when a reference changes hands.

title: The Complexity of Full-Information Iterated Protocols
summary: Full-information protocols are a common abstraction in distributed computing. In its iterated form, processes proceed through successive communication rounds in which each process shares its entire current knowledge of the execution. Usually, it is implicitly assumed that a process can transmit an unbounded amount of information in every round. This paper makes that assumption explicit and studies its computational cost. We formalize the problem of simulating iterated full-information protocols when communication is bounded, so that each process may share at most $b$ bits with every other process per round. We show that for a large family of shared-memory communication models and $n+1$ processes, simulating $r$ iterations of the full-information protocol requires \(\Omega\!\left((n!)^{r-1} 2^{\,n-b}\right)\) rounds. We complement this lower bound with simulation algorithms that are asymptotically optimal in the conventional read-write model. In particular, the case of two processes is special: $r$ iterations of a full-information protocol can be simulated in exactly $r$ rounds while using only $2$-bit variables, as the amount of information that must be represented remains bounded for two processes but grows with each iteration for $n \geq 2$.
comment: Journal version published in Theoretical Computer Science

title: One Structure Is Enough: Record-Native Tiles for Evolving Sparse Matrices on GPUs
summary: Sparse matrices that change over time, such as streaming graphs, are usually handled on GPUs with two parts: a packed format such as CSR, ELL, or SELL for computation, and a separate buffer for updates. Periodic maintenance then merges updates, rebuilds data, or changes formats. Our measurements show that this split is often unnecessary. We present RecTile, a tiled storage layer where each tile is kept in one sorted array of 12-byte edge records. For fragmented matrices, with 1 to 21 nonzeros per tile in our workloads, RecTile matches the best format-pinned slab tile at 0.56 to 1.21 times its time. Its tiled layout is also up to 21 times faster than whole-matrix cuSPARSE CSR. Specialized slabs are faster on the patterns they target at medium density, but both approaches converge by 25% density. RecTile stays within 1.1 to 1.6 times of whole-matrix cuSPARSE COO, our strongest static baseline, while COO cannot be updated in place. RecTile also uses no fixed per-tile device metadata for the stored matrix payload, so its tiles are smaller at realistic occupancies. A fully GPU-based ingest pipeline applies insert/delete/modify batches at up to 29 million edges per second, 4.5 times faster than the host path. An exact dynamic-programming oracle selects zero folds on every tested workload under its action space and calibrated cost model. Standard folding heuristics use 4 to 15 times more GPU time and up to 4 times more persistent device storage. End to end, RecTile improves the time-storage tradeoff on all five evolving-graph workloads, including delete-heavy streams. It is also fastest on a dense stress stream with 1220 records per tile. There, folding uses 1.3 times less peak persistent storage but takes 3.9 times more time. For the evolving graph-like, interleaved update/SpMV workloads evaluated here, the mutable record store can serve directly as the compute representation.

title: Placing the Control Plane: Cloud-Native Federated Learning Across Batch-Scheduled HPC
summary: The United Kingdom's AI Research Resource (AIRR) opens national supercomputers to a community familiar with always-reachable cloud services. With batch-scheduled HPC, a user requests a time-bounded allocation that is then reclaimed. Federated Learning (FL) exposes this tension, pairing a long-lived control plane with short-lived training. We characterize the resulting placement asymmetry: the coordination server sees only model updates and control metadata, so it can sit on neutral infrastructure, whereas the client control process is bound to the participating site's data and must remain within its trust boundary. The outbound-only connection this implies is also how edge clients connect, though the batch-scheduler mismatch is specific to HPC. We demonstrate a cross-silo federation spanning three independently administered systems (Isambard-AI, Isambard 3, and Zenith) using unmodified production FL frameworks (FLARE-wrapped Flower), measure the cost the client placement incurs, and propose Kubernetes-as-a-service as the in-boundary home for the persistent process.
comment: Accepted at The 1st International Workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO), co-located with SC26, Chicago, IL, USA, November 20, 2026. To appear in the SC26 Workshop Proceedings

title: CGSpec: Consistency-Guided Speculative Decoding with Overlap-Aware Verification Scheduling for Edge-Cloud Inference
summary: Collaborative speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by enabling edge clients to draft tokens locally and a shared cloud model to verify them. However, draft target disagreement wastes communication and verification resources, while heterogeneous client return times complicate shared verifier scheduling. We propose CGSpec, a consistency guided framework for multi client edge-cloud speculative decoding. CGSpec uses draft target distribution divergence to adapt the speculative budget and introduces a nomination and competition mechanism to construct candidate trees through global growth control and local token selection. An overlap-aware scheduler further estimates remaining verification work and client return times to prioritize requests and improve verifier utilization. We evaluate CGSpec using four model pairs and three datasets under heterogeneous network conditions. Across 24 configurations with 8 and 16 clients, CGSpec achieves the highest mean system and client throughput among the evaluated methods. Compared with current SOTA methods, it improves system throughput by 12.2\% and 10.2\%, and mean client throughput by 14.0\% and 33.0\%, respectively.

title: What Information Survives Authenticated Byzantine Communication?
summary: Two principals independently approve actions for a delegate that can choose a route to a goal and carry it out under current policy. A stable work-order receipt records the routes authorized at issuance. For intersection policies, we characterize the leading number of reachable joint configurations under overlapping updates. The lower bound uses the first writer's ability to finish before its peer invokes an update. The matching protocol checks an older route against the changed principal's policy because the unchanged principal already approved each of its steps. When each route has a command unique to it, the count has a closed form in terms of unions of route supports. Two three-command workflows with four possible receipts each have leading counts of $360$ and $328$ under encoded overwrite, and both have append count $1024$. Exact policy read-back forces at least six bits per block in both cases. Route overlap affects the count even when route lengths are fixed. The construction preserves authorization, withdrawal, stable recovery, and progress after stabilization with one coordinator crash.

title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
summary: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models
summary: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8\%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7\%.

title: Torcalia.jl: An MPI-based Runtime System for Asynchronous Task Parallelism in Julia
summary: Designed to address the two-language problem, the Julia programming language provides a powerful platform for developing high-performance scientific computing and machine learning applications. Such applications increasingly exhibit irregular, adaptive, or data-driven workloads for which traditional bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) models often struggle to efficiently exploit the available parallelism. Asynchronous many-task (AMT) runtime systems offer a compelling alternative, decomposing computations into fine-grained tasks that are dynamically scheduled across the hierarchical architecture of modern HPC systems. This paper introduces this http URL , a Julia package designed to orchestrate the asynchronous execution of tasks across both shared and distributed memory environments. Built on top of this http URL and Julia's native multithreading, Torcalia employs a dependency-aware task scheduling scheme that combines the work-sharing and work-stealing paradigms to achieve adaptive load balancing. Tasks can be nested arbitrarily, enabling applications to exploit multiple levels of parallelism, while application-level distributed shared memory (DSM) extends task-based shared-memory programming to multi-node clusters. Beyond task-based programming, the proposed library supports skeletal programming, providing high-level abstractions that facilitate the implementation of parallel applications at scale. Evaluated on the ARIS supercomputer using four diverse workloads, Torcalia demonstrates strong scalability, reducing wall-clock time by up to 18.1% compared with Dagger, a state-of-the-art task-based engine in Julia. The source code of this http URL is publicly available at this https URL .
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 4 listings. Source code: this https URL

title: Which $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ Algorithm is Suitable for You? An Empirical Benchmark on Real Network Traces
summary: Unreliable failure detectors (UFDs) are a fundamental abstraction for dependability and fault tolerance in distributed systems, supporting core distributed algorithms, such as consensus. Yet selecting a suitable detector remains difficult because existing implementations are evaluated under different environments, workloads, parameterizations, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We address this problem by systematizing 14 $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ and closely related $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$-style UFDs, implementing 13 of them, and providing a reusable benchmark for their empirical comparison. Our methodology evaluates detectors through common QoS metrics, such as detection time, mistake rate, and query accuracy, and combines same-input replay of network traces with live deployment for detectors whose active probing or cooperative behavior requires online execution. We then formalize failure-detector selection as a constrained algorithm-selection challenge, mapping operational requirements to suitable detector candidates. We instantiate this methodology under controlled variations of communication rate, host load, and crash regime. Applying the selection process shows that no detector is uniformly preferable across the evaluated settings. At relaxed detection-time budgets, 2W [Tomsic et al., IPDPS 2015] is the most frequently selected detector, appearing in 12 of 16 scenario-metric combinations for $T_D \le 500$ ms, whereas stricter budgets yield substantially more scenario- and metric-dependent selections. The benchmark and selection methodology provide a reusable basis for practical detector selection and for establishing stronger analytical baselines for future failure-detection approaches, including learning-based detectors.

title: X-BQSR: Holistic Acceleration of Base Quality Recalibration for Scalable Genomic Analysis
summary: With the continued decline in sequencing costs, genomics-based precision medicine is gaining increasing importance. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) is the standard framework for converting raw genomic data into actionable variants, but one of its most expensive steps is base quality score recalibration (BQSR), which corrects systematic sequencing errors. Despite significant work on accelerating other parts of the variant calling pipeline, BQSR has not been systematically explored on GPUs. In this work, we analyze BQSR to identify computational and I/O bottlenecks and show that simply offloading key stages to an accelerator is insufficient to achieve overall gains. We then present X-BQSR, a holistic redesign of the entire BQSR pipeline, including I/O, compression, and kernel execution, to better leverage GPU parallelism. We implement X-BQSR using portable SYCL kernels for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, along with native CUDA and HIP backends for comparison, and we evaluate its performance against previous FPGA work. Our evaluation shows up to 141.7x acceleration compared to standard GATK and 8.7x acceleration compared to a proprietary GPU-accelerated solution.

title: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions
summary: Byzantine Agreement protocols are traditionally designed under worst-case uncertainty about which processes are faulty, coupling the adversary's corruption budget $t$ with the system's epistemic uncertainty. Recent work showed that auxiliary failure predictions can improve round complexity, but cannot improve communication complexity when prediction errors are unconstrained. In this paper, we initiate a theoretical study of the complementary question: how much can Byzantine Agreement benefit when each process is guaranteed a local bound on its prediction error? We study this question through the local $k$-error prediction model, in which each process receives a local classification vector differing from the ground truth in at most $k$ positions. The predictions need not be common, and honest processes may hold substantially different views about whom to trust. Under this promise model -- where correctness relies on the local error bound holding -- we present a synchronous Byzantine Agreement algorithm requiring $n \ge t + 4k + 1$, where $n$ is the total number of processes, $t$ is the maximum number of failures, and $k$ is the local error bound per honest process. In the regime where local uncertainty is small ($k \ll t$), our protocol decouples communication from the total fault budget $t$: in an execution where the actual maximum prediction error is $s \le k$ and the actual number of failures is $f \le t$, the protocol terminates in $O(s+1)$ rounds and sends $O((f+k)ks + nk)$ honest messages, achieving $o(n^2)$ communication when $t = \Theta(n)$ and $k = o(\sqrt{n})$. Finally, we show that it is not possible to solve Byzantine Agreement in the local $k$-error prediction model with fewer than $\Omega(nk)$ honest messages.

title: Distributed Multimodal Monitoring and Prediction for PV Asset and Site Conditions
summary: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) monitoring remains fragmented: electrical performance, structural condition and vegetation management are typically assessed through separate workflows, making it difficult to relate changes in energy performance to the local physical and environmental conditions experienced by individual modules. We propose a distributed multimodal monitoring and prediction framework that combines mechanical, optical, electrical, and microclimate measurements at the string level. Rather than treating these measurements as independent sensor streams, the framework uses them to derive higher-level indicators of asset and site condition, including quantities that are not directly instrumented. We designed and installed four compact wireless nodes attached directly to the rear of PV modules for a three-month pilot study to demonstrate module-level monitoring. From low-cost multimodal measurements, the system detected vegetation-management events, predicted wind speed from module vibration on unseen data, and extracted repeatable structural-frequency fingerprints associated with individual module locations. These preliminary results demonstrate a pathway from distributed monitoring toward predictive PV asset management, where multimodal observations can be used to predict or estimate otherwise unobserved operating and structural states, identify emerging changes earlier, and provide more granular intelligence than plant-level electrical monitoring or periodic inspection alone.

title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
summary: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

title: HiPerfCC-KVCache: Accelerating Confidential LLM Serving with Hierarchical KV Caching
summary: Hierarchical key-value (KV) caching reduces repeated prefill computation in large language model serving by retaining reusable state beyond GPU memory. Under GPU confidential computing (CC), however, protected transfers can erase this benefit. We show that bulk KV copies hold driver locks during prolonged CPU-side processing, stalling independent serving operations despite separate threads and streams. Our characterization on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs shows how lock scope, copy granularity, and allocation ownership affect foreground progress and transfer parallelism. Guided by these findings, we present HiPerfCC-KVCache, which manages resource lifetimes, prioritizes ready token readback between bounded backup submissions, and parallelizes KV restores through auxiliary contexts with shared GPU staging. Implemented in SGLang, HiPerfCC-KVCache uses existing protected transfer interfaces without hardware or driver changes. Across three models and three workloads on H200, HiPerfCC-KVCache achieves a geometric-mean output-token throughput speedup of $1.74\times$ (up to $2.72\times$) over the staged KV-transfer HiCache-Workers baseline at the highest tested loads. Mean time to first token decreases by 36% on average and up to 59%. The benefits generalize to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, with a geometric-mean throughput speedup of $1.28\times$ (up to $2.20\times$) over the same baseline. A capacity analysis further models and explains variation in gains and remaining gaps to CC-off serving.

title: ARC: Adaptive Rollout Control for Efficient Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning
summary: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models proceeds through a repeated rollout--barrier--update loop. Each update must wait for a fixed number of complete, group-relative training samples, yet individual response lengths and reward outcomes vary widely and only emerge as generation progresses. Static admission and unconditional completion therefore leave accelerators idle in some steps, and waste computation generating samples that will never contribute to the current update. We present ARC, a closed-loop rollout architecture that governs synchronous RL rollout at group granularity. ARC uses \textit{Calibrated Streaming Backfill} to judge from partial observations whether a group is still worth completing, backfilling a fresh candidate immediately when it is not; \textit{Deferred Group Completion} to park an uncertain early stop and resume it later instead of discarding it outright, bounded by a resume-cycle limit that guarantees termination; and \textit{Adaptive Admission} and \textit{Pipelining} to order admitted samples by early-measured duration and to admit further candidates only while expected supply still falls short of the target number of accepted groups. Under online evaluation, ARC reduces rollout time by $37.4\%$, a $1.60\times$ speedup, and improves effective GRPO throughput by $50.1\%$ over existing baselines, while directly recovering 98.9\% of the training groups that would ultimately have been kept.

title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
summary: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

title: Two Rounds Are Already Hard for Loop-Free Updates of Routing Trees
summary: Updating a routing tree can create loops even when the old and new trees lead to the same destination. A controller chooses which routers update in each round, but their updates may finish in any order. Strong loop freedom therefore requires every partial completion to be acyclic. We show that deciding whether two rounds suffice is NP-complete, even when a safe three-round schedule is supplied. The proof is a linear-size reduction from 3-SAT with one old clause spine and four routers per variable. Three types of mixed cycles enforce consistent literal choices and clause satisfaction. For every nonempty input formula, the constructed instance needs exactly two rounds if the formula is satisfiable and exactly three otherwise.

title: Measuring GPU Memory Traffic on the NVIDIA GB10 Without C2C Telemetry
summary: The NVIDIA GB10, used in the DGX Spark and in desktop AI systems from several vendors, joins an Arm CPU die and a Blackwell GPU die with NVLink C2C. The GPU has no local memory, so every GPU access that misses in its L2 cache crosses C2C to the LPDDR5X attached to the CPU die. Yet the software on the systems we tested exposes no counter for this traffic. We show that five L2 sector counters of the GPU, sampled every 10 ms through NVIDIA's CUPTI sampling interface by a process that does not attach to the workload, measure GPU memory traffic live and separate copy engine traffic from the read misses and writes of GPU kernels. For large streaming transfers of known size, the counters agree within 0.28% on an Acer GN100 and within 0.005% on a DGX Spark, track the volume moved regardless of how it is split into copies, and exclude data reused in L2. The GPU's SMMU counter, a natural alternative, counts address translations rather than bytes. Applied to an unmodified server, the method shows Mistral 7B decode reading 13.47 GiB per token, the weights it uses plus its key value (KV) cache, at 83% of the memory bandwidth NVIDIA specifies. We release the method as an open source tool.

title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
summary: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
summary: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Author's submitted version (preprint) of paper accepted at ADBIS 2026 (European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems). The final authenticated version is available online at this https URL

title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
summary: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.

title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
summary: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.

title: WISP: Composable Representations for Wrist-Worn Activity Recognition
summary: Smartwatches and fitness bands are among the most common wearable devices, and large national health studies record movement at the wrist. Yet existing human activity recognition benchmarks mix sensors worn on different parts of the body, so they do not show how well activities can be recognised from the wrist alone. We introduce WristHARBench, a benchmark that standardises participant-disjoint evaluation across nine wrist-acceleration datasets and two additional multichannel inertial datasets. We hypothesise that different human activities leave complementary patterns in wrist motion, such as local shape, rhythm, temporal order and cross-axis relationships, and propose WISP (Wrist-Informed Space of Predictive Representations), a composable representation space that combines representations of these patterns with compatible classifiers. Across the nine primary datasets, WISP with random search achieves 70.20% mean Macro-F1, compared with 59.62% for the strongest of 18 external baselines. Controlled ablations and baseline comparisons indicate that recognition improves mainly when a representation adds motion patterns that the others lack, rather than when it represents the same pattern in a different way.

title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
summary: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

title: RefineKV: Query-Adaptive KV Cache Compression via Attention-Error Bounds
summary: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.

title: A world model for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction in older adults across multinational cohorts
summary: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.

title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
summary: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Code: this https URL

title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
summary: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

title: The Cross-Context Threshold Test: Detecting Discrimination Under Environmental Shifts
summary: We study how threshold tests for detecting discrimination under environmental shifts, focusing on the Veil-of-Darkness (VoD) setting where visibility changes between daylight and darkness. We show that standard threshold tests, when applied separately to daylight and darkness data, violate key assumptions: risk distributions drift across contexts and thresholds fluctuate arbitrarily. We propose a cross-context threshold test that enforces distributional invariance and monotonic threshold decay. Using New York City stop-and-frisk data and synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that this model yields more reliable thresholds, improves bias detection, and aligns with the counterfactual logic of the VoD test. Our framework generalizes to fairness auditing whenever environmental context influences decisions.

title: FoGConcept: Identifying Interpretable Movement Concepts for Freezing-of-Gait Detection from Multi-Scale IMU Signals
summary: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a disabling motor symptom of Parkinson's disease, characterized by an episodic inability to initiate or sustain effective stepping. Current inertial measurement unit (IMU)-based models can detect FoG accurately, but they fail to explain their predictions in terms of human-understandable movement concepts. A major contribution of this work is to identify nine human-understandable movement concepts encoded by a multi-scale FoG model, including gait initiation, rhythmic bilateral gait, trembling in place, shuffling steps, and pivot turns. These concepts recur across subjects, are functionally linked to the model's FoG decisions, and exhibit emergent specialization across short and long temporal contexts. Repeating the concept-discovery procedure on a new FoG dataset, wider temporal contexts, and a deeper backbone recovers the same comparatively stable set of movement concepts. Accordingly, we propose FoGConcept, a mechanism-based interpretability framework for learning movement concepts from multi-scale IMU signals. Domain experts independently recognize 88.9% of the identified concepts, while the proposed model achieves an F1 score of 94.2% for FoG detection. Our findings show that accurate FoG detection can be understood through human-recognizable movement patterns, providing new insight into what a detection model learns to distinguish FoG from non-FoG movement.

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
summary: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

title: SONATI: Spatio-temporal ocean neighbourhood asymmetric transformer for imputation of sparse, tabular data with uncertainty
summary: Missing value imputation is often a prerequisite for downstream analyses. In oceanography, observational data are frequently structured in a tabular manner, highly sparse and exhibit spatio-temporal structures that classical imputers such as k-nearest neighbours or MissForest are not suited to exploit. We present the Spatio-temporal Ocean Neighbourhood Asymmetric Transformer for Imputation (SONATI), a masked, factorised time-space transformer operating on pre-computed, local time and space neighbourhoods, which reduces computational complexity compared to global attention. SONATI is designed to work with tabular data and is thus in principle able to work on both gridded and unstructured data, though evaluation here was performed on gridded North Atlantic data only. It provides aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties through a negative log-likelihood loss and multiple forward passes with Monte Carlo dropout. Systematic ablations on attention type and masking strategies guided the final architecture design. The results showed that SONATI outperformed classical and transformer-based methods by at least 12.5% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) on a large observational oceanographic dataset with key biogeochemical and physical parameters in the North Atlantic (potential temperature, salinity, oxygen, nitrate, silicate and phosphate). Attention type and masking strategy strongly affected imputation accuracy and smoothness of the produced oceanographic fields. Best results were achieved by factorised time-space attention and combined geographic and per-sample masking. The combined masking strategy reduced the imputation error by 14.3% compared to per-sample masking only. Uncertainties were moderately well calibrated (miscalibration area at observed locations $0.074\pm0.012$) and moderately correlated with the imputation error.

title: What Do Differentiable Rule Learners Need? FLARE: Fuzzy Rules with Additive Evidence
summary: Rule learners are used where transparency and accountability are required, because they give practitioners patterns they can read. Learning rules is a discrete problem, so neurosymbolic pipelines that use rules as explanations rely on relaxations such as the straight-through estimator. However, these differentiable rule learners often lag behind both classical rule learners and black-box classifiers in terms of performance. We study which parts of a rule-based classifier affect performance, and how well gradient-based training learns each of them. We found that most of the performance comes from how the rules are weighted: random rules with learned weights are already more accurate than every published differentiable rule learner we tested. Based on our results, we propose FLARE (Fuzzy Learned-Antecedent Rule Evidence), a differentiable rule learner that learns simple rules that combine to make the final decision. We also propose a learned encoding for variables with thousands of categories. We test FLARE on tabular data, using 42 datasets of OpenML-CC18 and the 38 classification tasks of TabArena. On CC18, FLARE exceeds the compared rule learners by 7.69 to 12.38 macro-F1 points and performs comparably to random forests, while remaining 1.00 to 1.11 points below tuned gradient-boosted trees. On TabArena it ranks at the same level as random forests and ahead of the other rule learners. As the concept-to-label head of a concept bottleneck model, FLARE is the best rule-based head in five of six settings. On graphs, it is competitive on PubMed and EMOGI but falls behind graph neural networks on Cora and Citeseer. Our code is available at this https URL

title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
summary: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
comment: 40 pages, 15 figures, 12 tables. Code and checkpoints: this https URL

title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
summary: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures. Benchmark software and aggregate results (v1.0.0): this https URL . Curated EEG dataset (v1.0.0): this https URL

title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
summary: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027)

title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
summary: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. By learning a generalized structural bias over a diverse synthetic prior, TabK estimates the number of clusters in a single forward pass per ensemble member. Evaluated across 50 diverse real-world benchmarks, TabK outperforms all competing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) value of 1.04 compared to 2.14 for the closest competitor. TabK also achieves the lowest average inference time, producing estimates in less than one second on average and running $2\times$ faster than TabClustPFN and $30\times$ faster than traditional CVIs such as Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz. Code is available at this https URL .

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
summary: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices.
